text: You tap *BUY*. Two seconds later — order executed.
But in those 2 seconds, a stranger 1,000 km away
sold you his shares.
He doesn't know your name and you don't know his name.
And still nobody cheats anybody.
How?
Today we will follow one single trade, from the BUY button to your *demat account*,
and meet every institution that touches your money and your shares on the way.
By the end, you will understand the Indian stock market better than most people who trade every day.
Meet *Priya* — 28 years old, software engineer, stays in Pune.
She has finally decided to stop just watching finance reels
and actually invest.
She wants *10 shares* of a large IT company at *₹1,500* each.
Now meet *Mr. Kapoor*.
Retired bank officer, stays in Jaipur.
His granddaughter got admission to an engineering college.
and he wants to sell 10 shares of the same company to pay the fees.
Two people, two cities, *one trade*.
Let's see how they meet without ever meeting.
Before we move forward, a quick flashback. If Priya had done this in *1990*,
it would have been a very different story.
Shares were *paper certificates*.
Brokers shouted prices across a trading ring in Mumbai.
Certificates travelled by post. Signatures were checked by hand,
and a transfer could take *weeks*.
Fake certificates were a real risk.
Then came the *1992 securities scam*.
That same year, SEBI got statutory powers through the SEBI Act.
NSE started screen-based trading in *1994*,
and in *1996*, NSDL — India's first depository —
moved shares out of paper and into electronic form.
So the system Priya uses today was built because the old one *failed*.
Let's come back to today.
10 shares at ₹1,500.
Her broker is a SEBI-registered member of the exchange.
Priya can't walk into NSE herself.
The broker is her entry gate.
Before sending the order, the broker checks: does Priya have *₹15,000* available?
In Jaipur, Mr. Kapoor places a sell order.
His broker checks the 10 shares are in his demat account,
and he authorises the sale with a *TPIN or OTP*. No shares, no sale.
Both orders reach the stock exchange — NSE or BSE.
Think of the exchange as a giant digital marketplace.
Every buy order and sell order sits in an *order book*.
A computer matching engine
fills them on *price-time priority*:
best price first — and if prices are equal, whoever came first.
Priya buys at ₹1,500, meets Mr. Kapoor
selling at ₹1,500.
Matched in a fraction of a second,
and neither knows who the other is.
Now the most important player — the one nobody talks about: the *clearing corporation*.
NSE Clearing, or ICCL for BSE.
Here's the magic. Once the trade is matched,
the clearing corporation steps in the middle.
It becomes the buyer for Mr. Kapoor, and the seller for Priya.
This is called *novation*.
So what if Mr. Kapoor's broker defaults tomorrow?
Priya will still receive her shares, because her
counterparty is now the clearing corporation,
backed by *margins* and a *settlement guarantee fund*.
That is why two strangers can trade without trusting each other — because they trust the *system*.
Next is *settlement*, where the money and shares actually move.
India follows *T+1* settlement:
trade day plus 1 working day.
Priya buys on Monday. By Tuesday, the shares move out of Mr. Kapoor's demat account
through the depository — NSDL or CDSL.
Since *October 2024*,
they are credited *directly* into Priya's demat account by the clearing corporation,
not parked with the broker.
On the same day, the money moves through clearing banks,
and Mr. Kapoor receives his ₹15,000, minus charges and taxes.
India even has optional same-day — *T+0* — settlement
for the top 500 stocks.
Now, where do *banks* fit in? Wherever money moves, a bank gets involved.
Priya's bank holds her money and transfers it to her broker.
Large brokers must now also offer a *UPI block* option,
where her money stays blocked in her own bank account
and is debited only when the trade settles — just like ASBA in IPOs.
Behind the scenes, *clearing banks* move funds between brokers and the clearing corporation every day.
Now, what if the buyer is not Priya, but a mutual fund or a foreign investor buying
*₹500 crore* of shares?
They use a *custodian* — usually a large bank registered with SEBI.
Think of the custodian as a high-security locker
plus a back office for institutions. It holds their securities
safely,
settles their trades with the clearing corporation,
collects dividends,
handles bonuses and splits,
and reports everything back.
Retail investors like Priya don't need one.
Their brokers and depository participants do this job.
We have seen that so many players are involved in the Indian stock market,
so there is a need for a regulator — and *SEBI* creates the rules for every party involved.
SEBI registers every player,
monitors trading and punishes wrongdoing. For example, in 2019 a big broker, *Karvy*, misused client shares. SEBI barred Karvy in 2019 over defaults of around *₹2,000 crore*,
and later cancelled its registration.
After that, SEBI tightened the rules.
Client shares can't be *pooled* with the broker anymore,
and they now go straight into your demat account.
That is why around *23 crore* demat accounts can trust a system where buyers and sellers are total strangers.
So: one trade, one relay race. The broker takes your order, the exchange matches it, the clearing corporation
guarantees it, the depository moves the shares,
the bank moves the money, the custodian does it for big institutions — and SEBI watches everyone.
Priya got her shares. Mr. Kapoor paid the college fees.
And they will never know each other's name.
